lead: A worm drive is a screw, the worm, turning a gear, the worm wheel, on a shaft at right angles to it. One stage gives a large reduction, 10:1 to 80:1, because the worm has only one to four threads (starts) while the wheel has many teeth. Contact is mostly sliding, so friction, wear and heat set the size more than tooth bending does. Worm drives turn lift winches, conveyor reducers, steering boxes and indexing tables.
prereq: You need: the Lewis equation of spur gear design, the steel-bronze pair of gear materials, and the efficiency of a power screw.

sections.h3: Geometry: the worm sets the size

blocks.text: Let the worm have z1 starts and the wheel z2 teeth. The speed ratio is i = n1/n2 = z2/z1. The worm's axial pitch pa equals the wheel's circular pitch, πm, where m is the module (axial module of the worm, transverse module of the wheel). The lead is the distance the thread advances in one turn: L = z1 pa = z1πm.

The worm's pitch diameter is not m z1. It is set by the diametral quotient q (some syllabi call it the worm factor): d1 = qm, with q usually 8 to 12. The wheel diameter is d2 = m z2 and the centre distance a = (d1 + d2)/2. The lead angle λ is the angle between the thread and a plane normal to the worm axis, measured on the pitch cylinder:

blocks.where: So a small q gives a slender worm and a large lead angle; a large q gives a thick, stiff worm and a small lead angle. Adding starts raises the lead and the lead angle.

blocks.text: The worm's pitch line velocity is v1 = πd1n_1/60 (d1 in m). The thread slides along the wheel tooth at the rubbing velocity vs = v1/cos λ, larger than v1. Friction is written as a coefficient μ, or as a friction angle φ = tan⁻¹μ; μ falls as vs rises and is about 0.02 to 0.05 for a well-lubricated steel worm on a bronze wheel.

η = (cos αn − μ tan λ)/(cos αn + μ cot λ) η is the efficiency with the worm driving and αn the normal pressure angle (often 20°). If αn is ignored, as many books do, it becomes η = tan λ/tan(λ + φ), the efficiency of a square-threaded screw.

The drive is self-locking when the wheel cannot turn the worm, roughly when λ < φ (more exactly when μ > cos αn tan λ). A self-locking hoist holds its load without a brake, but its forward efficiency is then below 50 %, so much of the power becomes heat. The worm is case-hardened and ground steel; the wheel is phosphor bronze, because the pair must slide without seizing.

The worm's tangential force F<sub>t1</sub> = 2T<sub>1</sub>/d<sub>1</sub> equals the axial thrust on the wheel. The wheel's tangential force F<sub>t2</sub> = 2T<sub>2</sub>/d<sub>2</sub> equals the axial thrust on the worm. The two are related through λ and μ: F<sub>t2</sub> = F<sub>t1</sub> (cos α<sub>n</sub> cos λ − μ sin λ)/(cos α<sub>n</sub> sin λ + μ cos λ). The separating force is F<sub>r</sub> = F<sub>t1</sub> sin α<sub>n</sub>/(cos α<sub>n</sub> sin λ + μ cos λ).

items: Bending: the bronze wheel tooth is the weaker. A common textbook form is Sb = σb b mn Y, with mn = m cos λ, Y read for z2, and a velocity factor Cv = 6/(6 + v2) on the wheel's pitch line velocity v2; check Sb ≥ Ft2/Cv.
Wear: the contact stress of the steel-bronze pair limits the face width; data books give a limiting wear load in terms of d2, b and a wear factor for the pair and lead angle.

Heat: the power lost is (1 − η)P. In steady running it must leave through the housing: (1 − η)P = k A (t − t0), where k is the heat transfer coefficient in W/(m²K), A the housing area in m², t the oil temperature and t0 the air temperature. Oil should stay below about 80 °C; a fan on the worm shaft roughly doubles k.

blocks.text: A small worm box often has strong teeth and still overheats, so for continuous duty the heat check usually decides the catalogue power. The same heat balance is used for whole gearboxes in gearbox design.

figure.caption: Worm efficiency computed for a normal pressure angle of 20°. Efficiency rises steeply with lead angle, so a single-start worm loses about a quarter of its power as heat while four starts lose far less.

spec.aria: Two efficiency curves against lead angle for friction 0.03 and 0.10, with points at 5.71 degrees, 75.6 per cent and 21.8 degrees.

examples.question: A single-start worm (z<sub>1</sub> = 1) with module 5 mm and q = 10 drives a 40-tooth wheel; the worm turns at 1440 rpm. Find d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>, a, the lead, the lead angle, v<sub>1</sub> and the rubbing velocity.
steps: Lead angle: tan λ = z<sub>1</sub>/q = 1/10 = 0.1, so λ = 5.711°.
Worm pitch line velocity: v<sub>1</sub> = π × 0.050 × 1440/60 = 3.770 m/s.
Rubbing velocity: v<sub>s</sub> = 3.770/cos 5.711° = 3.770/0.99504 = 3.789 m/s. Ratio i = 40 and wheel speed 1440/40 = 36 rpm.
examples.answer: d<sub>1</sub> = 50 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 200 mm, a = 125 mm, L = 15.71 mm, λ = 5.71°, v<sub>1</sub> = 3.77 m/s, v<sub>s</sub> = 3.79 m/s.

examples.question: The drive of the first example takes 2 kW. Take μ = 0.03 and α<sub>n</sub> = 20°. Find the efficiency, the wheel torque, the forces on the worm, and whether the drive is self-locking. For the bronze wheel σ<sub>b</sub> = 80 N/mm² and b = 40 mm: check bending. The housing has 0.6 m² of surface, k = 15 W/(m²K) in still air and 25 W/(m²K) with a fan, air at 35 °C: find the oil temperature.
steps: Worm torque: T<sub>1</sub> = 2000 × 60/(2π × 1440) = 13.26 N·m; F<sub>t1</sub> = 2 × 13.26/0.050 = 530.5 N (this is also the wheel's axial thrust).
Wheel torque: T<sub>2</sub> = ηP/ω<sub>2</sub> = 0.756 × 2000/(2π × 36/60) = 400.9 N·m; F<sub>t2</sub> = 2 × 400.9/0.200 = 4009 N (the worm's axial thrust).
Self-locking: φ = tan⁻¹0.03 = 1.72° is less than λ = 5.71°, so the wheel can drive the worm back. The drive is not self-locking and needs a brake on a hoist.
Heat: loss = (1 − 0.756) × 2000 = 489 W. Still air: t − t<sub>0</sub> = 489/(15 × 0.6) = 54.3 K, oil at 89 °C, too hot. With a fan: 489/(25 × 0.6) = 32.6 K, oil at 68 °C, acceptable.
examples.answer: η = 75.6 %, T<sub>2</sub> = 400.9 N·m, F<sub>t1</sub> = 530.5 N, F<sub>t2</sub> = 4009 N, F<sub>r</sub> = 1471 N; not self-locking; bending factor 1.54; the oil reaches 89 °C in still air, so fit a fan (68 °C).

traps: Taking d<sub>1</sub> = m z<sub>1</sub>. The worm is a screw: d<sub>1</sub> = qm.
Reversing the ratio: i = z<sub>2</sub>/z<sub>1</sub>, not z<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>2</sub>.
Putting the pressure angle in place of the friction angle in η = tan λ/tan(λ + φ).
Forgetting the starts: L = z<sub>1</sub>πm, so a two-start worm has twice the lead and a larger lead angle.
Self-locking means λ < φ, roughly; it brings an efficiency below 50 % and is not a sign of good design. Swapping the thrusts: the worm's axial thrust equals the wheel's tangential force.

quiz.q: Define the lead angle of a worm.
quiz.a: The angle between the worm thread and a plane normal to the worm axis, on the pitch cylinder: tan λ = L/(πd<sub>1</sub>) = z<sub>1</sub>/q.

quiz.q: Why is the worm diameter qm and not m z<sub>1</sub>?
quiz.a: The worm is a screw; its diameter is chosen to make it stiff enough and to give a suitable lead angle, through q. m z<sub>1</sub> would describe a spur gear.

quiz.q: Why is the rubbing velocity larger than the worm's pitch line velocity?
quiz.a: The thread is inclined at λ, so the relative sliding is along the thread: v<sub>s</sub> = v<sub>1</sub>/cos λ.

quiz.q: A two-start worm has m = 4 mm, q = 12 and drives a 60-tooth wheel. Find d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>, i, L and λ.
A worm has λ = 4° and μ = 0.10. Is it self-locking?
quiz.a: φ = tan⁻¹0.10 = 5.71° > λ = 4°, so it is self-locking: the wheel cannot drive the worm.

quiz.q: At λ = 10°, compare η = tan λ/tan(λ + φ) for φ = 6° and φ = 3°.
quiz.a: tan 10°/tan 16° = 0.1763/0.2867 = 0.615; tan 10°/tan 13° = 0.1763/0.2309 = 0.764. Halving the friction angle raises the efficiency by about 15 percentage points, which is why lubrication matters so much.

quiz.q: A worm box passes the bending check but its oil reaches 95 °C. What will you change?
quiz.a: The heat check governs. Add fins or a fan to raise kA, use a larger housing, use an oil with lower friction, or raise the lead angle (more starts) to raise the efficiency.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial worm boxes use double-enveloping (globoid) worms that wrap more wheel teeth and carry more load. Catalogue ratings for continuous duty are usually thermal ratings. Search for globoid worm gear, worm gear thermal rating and synthetic gear oils for worm drives.
